articles.title: Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood
articles.raw_summary: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. articles.title: How to make a moral agent: sentimentalism and rationalism as lenses on AI
articles.raw_summary: Can AI systems be moral agents? That is, can they undertake actions that can be correctly assessed as morally right or wrong? There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies neatly outside paradigm human cases. Because of the difficulties with a normative account, we instead propose a research program to explore descriptive moral agency. Most basically, we ask, what are the capabilities we humans possess that underlie our moral agency? articles.title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
articles.raw_summary: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. articles.title: Skill-Latent Rewards: LLM-Guided Reward Formulation for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
articles.raw_summary: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process.

articles.title: Not All Data Leakage Is Equal: A Controlled Benchmark of Evaluation Inflation in Tabular Classification
articles.raw_summary: Data leakage is widely recognized as a threat to trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, yet the phrase covers mechanisms with very different statistical consequences.
